summary: Thin day: Reddit, X and Bluesky were blocked and web search surfaced no primary posts, so only Hacker News threads could be verified. The strongest signals were Microsoft's To Do shutdown stranding simple-list users, macOS Full Disk Access prompts that nobody can interpret, and self-hosted services that non-technical friends and family cannot be asked to run.

ideas.title: Simple Shared Lists with One-Tap Microsoft To Do Import
ideas.oneLiner: A calm, Wunderlist-style list app (shopping, chores, simple tasks) that imports your Microsoft To Do data in one tap before it shuts down.
ideas.problem: Microsoft is retiring To Do and telling users to choose another app. People who used it as a plain shopping or chore list now need a replacement, and previous Microsoft migrations (Wunderlist to To Do) lost data or locked users out. Existing alternatives are either heavy project managers or paywalled.
ideas.targetUsers: Casual users of Microsoft To Do for shopping lists, household chores and personal reminders; couples and families sharing lists.
ideas.monetization: Free for personal lists with unlimited items; ₹99/month or ₹799/year for shared households, reminders and attachments.
mvp: Microsoft account sign-in and import of lists, tasks, due dates and notes
Plain lists with check-off, drag reorder and offline support
Share a list with one other person via a link
Location or time reminders for shopping lists
Export to CSV/JSON so users never get locked in

competitors.name: Todoist
competitors.gap: Capable but paid features and a project-manager feel; one commenter is a happy paying user, but others want something simpler.

competitors.name: Vikunja
competitors.gap: Needs self-hosting on a VPS, which most To Do users will not do.

competitors.name: Google Tasks
competitors.gap: Minimal sharing and no import from Microsoft To Do.

ideas.title: Mac Permission Translator
ideas.oneLiner: A menu-bar app that shows which apps hold Full Disk Access and other privacy permissions, in plain language, with one-click revoke and a risk note per app.
ideas.problem: macOS permission prompts are vague, and Apple is tightening Full Disk Access just as AI agents and chat apps ask for it. Users cannot tell what a permission really grants or whether an app has any business asking.
ideas.targetUsers: Mac users who are not security experts, and developers who install many AI tools and CLIs.
ideas.monetization: Free scan; ₹1,500 one-time (or about $19) for continuous monitoring, change alerts and per-app history.
mvp: List every app with Full Disk Access, Accessibility, Screen Recording and similar grants, read from the TCC database where permitted
Plain-language explanation of what each permission lets an app do
Flag apps whose category does not usually need a permission (for example a chat client with Full Disk Access)
Deep link to the exact System Settings pane to revoke
Alert when a new app gains a sensitive permission

competitors.name: macOS System Settings > Privacy & Security
competitors.gap: Lists grants but explains nothing and gives no context on risk.

competitors.name: Objective-See tools (LuLu, KnockKnock)
competitors.gap: Powerful but aimed at security-minded users, with no plain-language permission explainer.

ideas.title: Self-Host Keeper: Backups and Health Checks for Services You Run for Others
ideas.oneLiner: A tiny agent plus dashboard that verifies backups restore, certificates and domains stay valid, and pings you in plain language when a service you host for family or friends breaks.
ideas.problem: Self-hosting works for hobbyists, but reliability, networking and backups are where it falls down, and recommending it to non-technical people is hard. The person running the server becomes unpaid support, and a silent failure loses data.
ideas.targetUsers: Hobbyists who self-host Vaultwarden, Immich, Matrix or similar for family and friends, and small teams on a rented VPS.
ideas.monetization: Free for one server; $5/month for unlimited servers, restore tests and WhatsApp/Telegram alerts.
mvp: One-line agent install that detects common self-hosted apps via Docker labels
Nightly backup check that actually test-restores a sample and reports failure
Certificate, domain and disk-space expiry warnings
Weekly plain-language status message for a non-technical family member

competitors.name: Uptime Kuma
competitors.gap: Checks that things are up, but does not verify that backups can be restored.

competitors.name: Healthchecks.io
competitors.gap: Cron monitoring only; no app discovery or restore verification.
